hook.text: In 1986, a ceramic shattered physics — it conducted electricity with zero resistance.

buildup.text: Metal superconductors needed liquid helium at 4 K. Ceramics worked at 77 K — liquid nitrogen.

discovery.text: Copper-oxide ceramics like YBCO achieved 'high-temperature' superconductivity no one expected.

twist.text: Ceramics are brittle — making flexible wires from them remains one of engineering's toughest challenges.

climax.text: MRI machines use superconducting coils to generate the powerful magnets that image your body.

punchline.text: The most unexpected conductor turned out to be ceramic.

quiz.question: Why were ceramic superconductors a breakthrough?
options: They worked at higher temperatures than metal superconductors
They were cheaper to make than metal wires
They could be bent like copper wire
